questions.q: What is the fundamental difference between how Slurm and Kubernetes approach running workloads?
options: Slurm only supports CPU workloads, Kubernetes only supports GPU workloads
Slurm is built around batch jobs that run to completion and stop; Kubernetes is built around long-running services that reconcile toward a declared state
Slurm requires cloud infrastructure; Kubernetes only runs on-premises
There is no meaningful difference — they are interchangeable APIs for the same scheduler
questions.explain: Slurm's model is batch jobs: submit, run, finish, stop. Kubernetes is built around continuously reconciling a declared state, which is why training (a long batch job) and services (long-running) fit each system differently.

questions.q: In the sbatch script, what do --nodes=64 and --gres=gpu:8 together request?
options: 64 total GPUs across any number of nodes
8 nodes with 64 GPUs each
64 nodes with 8 GPUs each, for 512 GPUs total
A single node reserved exclusively for 64 hours
questions.explain: --nodes=64 requests 64 nodes, and --gres=gpu:8 requests 8 GPUs on each of them — 512 GPUs total, the same scale as the PyTorchJob example.

questions.q: What is the difference between sbatch and srun?
options: sbatch submits a batch script and returns immediately, running whenever Slurm schedules it; srun launches a command across nodes already allocated to a job
They are two names for the exact same command
sbatch is for GPU jobs, srun is for CPU-only jobs
srun submits to the queue; sbatch only works interactively
questions.explain: sbatch queues a batch job and hands control back to the user right away. srun is what actually starts a command on the nodes once an allocation exists — used both inside batch scripts and interactively.

questions.q: Why does the sbatch script set #SBATCH --time=72:00:00 deliberately rather than leaving it unset?
options: It has no real effect and is purely cosmetic
Slurm kills a job once it exceeds its wall-clock time limit, so a long training run needs that limit set intentionally
It controls how many GPUs are requested
It sets how often checkpoints are saved
questions.explain: The --time directive is a hard wall-clock limit; Slurm terminates the job once it's exceeded, so a multi-day training run must set it to cover the expected runtime.

questions.q: What is a Slurm partition most analogous to in Kubernetes terms?
options: A Kubernetes Namespace
A node pool — a named subset of cluster nodes with its own rules — except Slurm's own scheduler, not Kubernetes', decides what runs on it
A single Pod
A ConfigMap
questions.explain: A partition groups a subset of nodes under its own scheduling rules, similar in concept to a node pool, but it is scheduled entirely by Slurm rather than by the Kubernetes scheduler.
